frequency_question: How often do states successfully establish domestic production lines for transferred advanced cruise missiles or precision-guided munitions under wartime pressure within a 2-to-3-year window?
membership_rule: Includes instances of foreign-origin advanced missile systems where local assembly or component manufacturing lines were initiated and achieved operational status during active conflict or extreme urgency. Excludes standard licensed production in stable, allied nations during peacetime (e.g., F-16s built in South Korea or Turkey over decades).

cases.name: Egypt domestic assembly of Soviet/Chinese anti-ship missiles (Soviets expelled, pivot to domestic/Chinese)
Taiwan Hsiung Feng missile series (rapid indigenous production from Israeli/foreign blueprints under diplomatic isolation)
South Africa Project Y/Kentron advanced munitions under arms embargo
Pakistan Anza missile production (licensed/reverse-engineered Chinese designs)
Iran Noor/Qader cruise missile production from C-802 blueprints

coverage_note: 5 named historical analogues representing severe technological transfer and wartime urgency constraints.
known_gaps: Modern Western cruise missile tech transfer (such as Storm Shadow/SCALP) involves vastly more complex microelectronics, proprietary software source codes, and specialized material science than 1980s/1990s missile systems, introducing higher structural friction than historical baselines.
skeleton: 5 documented major historical attempts by nations facing acute external supply friction to stand up domestic guided-missile or precision-weapon lines under duress.
multiplier: 4 hits out of 5 historical instances where states successfully engineered or transferred production under severe structural friction.
validity_reason: Based on historical precedents of defense industrial mobilization under sanctions or war, which evolve slowly over decades.
